title: Tidy Tuesday: Global Health Spending
text:
This analysis uses the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database (GHED), which includes data on health spending for 195 countries from 2000 to 2023. The dataset shows how much countries spend on health care and where that funding comes from, including government spending, private sources, and external aid.
The main question guiding this analysis is:
Can we predict a country’s out-of-pocket payment burden (as a percentage of total health spending) based on the share of funding from government, private, and external sources?
This question matters for public health because high out-of-pocket costs can make it harder for people to access care and may lead to financial strain. This is especially true in low- and middle-income countries (World Health Organization, 2024), where individuals often bear a larger share of health care costs.

The random forest model performed the best, with the lowest RMSE and highest R² out of the three models. I selected it as the final model because it can capture more complex, non-linear relationships between different sources of health spending and out-of-pocket burden. This makes sense given how varied health financing systems are across countries with different income levels and structures. While linear regression is easier to interpret, the better predictive performance of the random forest makes it a stronger choice for this analysis.

title: Tidy Tuesday: Global Health Spending
text:
Discussion
This analysis used WHO global health spending data to examine whether a country’s out-of-pocket (OOP) payment burden can be predicted based on its mix of government, private, and external health spending.
The random forest model performed the best, with a cross-validated RMSE of 6.45 and an R² of 0.895. It performed even better on the test set, with an RMSE of 6.06 and an R² of 0.913, meaning the model explained about 91% of the variation in OOP burden on data it had never seen before.
Government spending share was the strongest predictor of OOP burden. Countries that rely more on government funding tend to have lower out-of-pocket costs for individuals, since public financing reduces direct payments at the point of care. This aligns with long-standing research showing that expanding public health coverage is one of the most effective ways to reduce financial hardship (World Health Organization, 2024).
The EDA showed a general decline in OOP burden globally from 2000 to 2023, reflecting progress toward universal health coverage. However, many countries in South and Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa still have OOP burdens above 60% of total health spending, which remains a major concern.
One limitation is that this analysis treats each country-year as independent, even though repeated observations from the same country are likely correlated. A more rigorous approach would account for this clustering using mixed effects models.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
2.1 Research Question
Are individuals who report being asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal care less likely to report postpartum depressive symptoms?
The primary outcome is self-reported postpartum depressive symptoms, measured using PRAMS survey items assessing feelings of depression and loss of interest since birth. The primary predictor is prenatal mental health screening, defined as whether a healthcare provider asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal visits. Additional covariates include depression during pregnancy and maternal education.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.1 Use of Computational Assistance
ChatGPT was used to help troubleshoot parts of the code. All analyses, decisions, and interpretations were reviewed and completed by the author.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.2 Analysis Approach
The analysis started by comparing people who reported having prenatal mental health screening with those who did not. This helped us check the data for quality, find missing details, and identify early patterns. We then used statistical methods to explore the relationship between prenatal screening and postpartum depression, taking into account important factors.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.3 Data Source
Data came from PRAMS, a survey system run by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention along with state health departments. PRAMS gathers information that people report about their experiences before, during, and shortly after pregnancy. Because PRAMS uses a detailed survey method, the data can be analyzed using special variables included in the dataset. The analyses shown here are unweighted and intended as a simple example of how to build models so others can repeat them.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.4 Study Population
The full PRAMS analytic dataset included 237,392 respondents. After excluding observations with missing values for the primary exposure, outcome, and selected covariates, the final analytic sample included 233,213 respondents. Complete case analysis was used, which might cause bias if data are not missing completely at random. Respondents with missing data might differ in important ways from those with complete data, potentially affecting how well the results apply to other groups. title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.5 Measures
The main exposure was whether a healthcare provider talked about depression or anxiety during prenatal visits, based on a survey question. This was recorded as yes or no. The main outcome was postpartum depressive symptoms, measured using survey questions about feelings of depression and loss of interest after childbirth. These questions have been used before in research on postpartum depression Bauman et al. (2020); Farr et al. (2016). Key factors were depression during pregnancy and the mother’s education level. Depression during pregnancy was included because women who have had depression before are more likely to have depressive symptoms after giving birth. The mother’s education was included because it can affect access to healthcare and mental health.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.6 Statistical Approach
Exploratory analyses involved looking at basic statistics, cross-tabulation, and bar charts to compare postpartum depression symptoms based on screening status. All work was done using R. A multivariable logistic regression was used to analyze whether postpartum depression symptoms were linked to prenatal mental health screening. Depression during pregnancy and maternal education were included as additional factors. Results are shown as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
A random forest approach was also used alongside logistic regression because it can handle complex relationships between variables without needing to specify them in advance. To see if this method improved prediction, both models were tested using 5-fold cross-validation. The random forest used the ranger package with 300 trees and default settings for other options. The performance of the models was measured by accuracy and ROC AUC, with averages and variation across the tests used to check stability.

library(tidyverse)

raw <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("cdcdata-exercise", "cdc_obesity_2018plus.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
stopifnot(nrow(raw) > 0)


dat <- raw %>% # saves raw data as dat for next steps in synth creation
  transmute( # creates new dataset with same variables as in original, with cleaned names and formatting
    year = YearStart,
    state = LocationAbbr,
    location = LocationDesc,
    question = Question,
    value = Data_Value,
    unit = Data_Value_Unit,
    value_type = Data_Value_Type,
    sex = Sex,
    age_group = `Age(years)`
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, ""))) %>% # if values are empty strings, convert to NA for consistency in handling missing data
  filter(!is.na(value)) # removes rows where value var is missing


# Reproducibility: set seed for any random processes
set.seed(1234) # original seed was 2026, changed it because i prefer simple numbers.
# Reproducibility
set.seed(1234)

# Ensure Part 1 object exists
stopifnot(exists("dat"))

# helper: sample from observed distribution including NA
# helper makes synthetic data preserve the same distribution of values (including missingness) as the original data
sample_like <- function(x, n) {
  tx <- table(x, useNA = "ifany") # counts how often each value (including NA) appears in the original data
  p  <- as.numeric(tx) / sum(tx) # coverts counts to probabilities/proportions
  lv <- names(tx) # saves the unique values (including NA) as a character vector
  s  <- sample(lv, size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = p)
  ifelse(s == "<NA>", NA, s) # converts string "<NA>" back to actual NA values in the synthetic data
}

n_rows <- nrow(dat) # stores the number of rows in the original dataset so synth dataset can copy.

# keep valid state-location pairs
state_location_map <- dat %>%
  filter(!is.na(state), !is.na(location)) %>%
  distinct(state, location)

# build synthetic scaffold (without value first)
dat_syn <- tibble(
  year       = as.numeric(sample_like(dat$year, n_rows)),
  state      = sample_like(dat$state, n_rows),
  question   = sample_like(dat$question, n_rows),
  unit       = sample_like(dat$unit, n_rows),
  value_type = sample_like(dat$value_type, n_rows),
  sex        = sample_like(dat$sex, n_rows),
  age_group  = sample_like(dat$age_group, n_rows)
) %>%
  left_join(state_location_map, by = "state")

# fallback if any missing locations remain
if (any(is.na(dat_syn$location))) {
  dat_syn$location[is.na(dat_syn$location)] <-
    sample_like(dat$location, sum(is.na(dat_syn$location))) # fills in any missing locations by sampling from the original location distribution, ensuring all rows have a location value.
}

# Simulate value using subgroup stats + global fallback
g_mean <- mean(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)
g_sd   <- sd(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)
v_min  <- min(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)
v_max  <- max(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)

# subgroup means/sd by question + sex + age group

grp <- dat %>%
  group_by(question, sex, age_group) %>%
  summarise(
    mu = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"

  left_join(grp, by = c("question", "sex", "age_group")) %>%
  mutate(
    mu = ifelse(is.na(mu), g_mean, mu),
    sd = ifelse(is.na(sd) | sd <= 0, g_sd, sd),
    value = rnorm(n(), mean = mu, sd = sd),
    value = pmax(v_min, pmin(v_max, value))
  ) %>%
